original_candidates.sentence: Spanish builds a comparable family term the opposite direction, by contraction rather than suffixing: [mijo](/mijo-meaning/) squeezes mi hijo, "my son," into one word used to address a child or close friend, an entirely separate history from the identically spelled word for a cereal grain.

That two-sense structure, one word doing both jobs depending on who\'s speaking to whom, is the same shape [habibi](/habibi-meaning/) has in Arabic, where a term built for close relationships also gets used, in a different register, for someone the speaker barely knows.

Whatever nuance Spanish preserves by keeping "little mama" and "hottie" as two clearly labeled senses of the same word, English flattened into one, the same narrowing [voilà](/voila-meaning/) underwent when it crossed into English and kept only its dramatic-reveal sense, dropping the French word\'s separate use for marking elapsed time.

original_candidates.sentence: Japanese farewells hide a similar gap between literal pieces and everyday translation: [sayonara](/sayonara-meaning/) is glossed as a simple "goodbye," but its literal sense is closer to "if that\'s how it is," and unlike a casual arigatō, it signals a long or permanent parting rather than an everyday one.
